title: Nitrogen Use Efficiency in Dairy Breeding
text: Welcome

title: Nitrogen Use Efficiency in Dairy Breeding
text:
The question
Dairy cows turn only part of the nitrogen they eat into milk protein; the rest leaves the farm as urine and faeces. The Nordic Total Merit index (NTM) does not weigh NUE directly. So the central question is:

If NUE is added to the NTM breeding goal, how much NUE is gained, and what does it cost in total merit, methane and inbreeding?

title: Nitrogen Use Efficiency in Dairy Breeding
text:
The answer in one table
Responses are over the simulated selection period. Differences are paired within replicate (10 replicates, each with its own founder population). Significance here follows the Benjamini-Hochberg correction explained in 8  Statistics and multiple testing.







Question
Result




Does NTM alone improve NUE?
Yes, by 3.3 to 3.4 genetic SD in all breeds, but only through NUE’s genetic correlations with yield. With those correlations set to 0, the gain is about 0.


What does an explicit NUE weight add?
Weight 0.35: HOL +1.08, JER +0.94, RDC +0.82 SD of NUE, significant in all three breeds. Weight 0.75: +0.95 to +1.43 SD.


What does the NUE weight cost in NTM?
Too small to detect at weight 0.35: theory predicts about 1.3 to 1.6 index units, and the replicate SD of the difference is 5 to 6 units.


What happens to methane?
Methane rises 1.6 to 2.1 SD under NTM alone. A methane weight of -0.5 lowers it by 1.4 to 1.6 SD, at about EUR 28 to 39 per cow-year (the cost passes correction in HOL and JER only).


Does selecting against milk urea (MUN) help NUE?
No. MUN falls 1.2 to 1.4 SD and NUE does not change.


Can inbreeding be controlled?
Unconstrained genomic selection: 1.8 to 2.2% per generation. Optimum contribution selection: 0.7 to 1.0%.


Is there genotype x country interaction?
It could not be estimated reliably at this sample size.

title: 1  The question and the population
text:
1.1 Nitrogen use efficiency and the breeding goal
NUE is the share of nitrogen intake that a cow puts into milk protein. It can be predicted on farm from feed intake, diet crude protein and milk protein, which is why large-scale feed-intake recording makes a genetic evaluation of NUE realistic.
The Nordic Total Merit index (NTM) combines sub-indices for yield, fertility, udder health, longevity, Saved Feed and other traits. It has no weight on NUE, milk urea or methane. The simulation therefore compares the current NTM goal with versions that add NUE, milk urea or methane on top.

title: 1  The question and the population
text:
1.2 Population sizes
The CFIT cow numbers (28,400 cows across 4 countries) reported in the Cattle FeedInTake presentation by Jan Lassen and Søren Borchersen were used (source).
These values have similar breed proportions to the ICAR 2026 (Verona) report of 25,614 cows (10,914 Holstein, 7,542 Jersey, 7,158 Red Dairy Cattle) on more than 30 commercial farms in Denmark, Finland, Sweden and Germany, with 1,282,122 weekly records.
Breed sizes reported by VikingGenetics (523,000 Holstein, 121,000 Jersey, 76,000 Red Dairy) were not used: they carry no information on CFIT records, over-weight Holstein (72.6%) relative to the CFIT data (42.6%), and exclude the German data.

title: 1  The question and the population
text:
1.3 Germany and the NAV evaluation
The NAV documentation (May 2024) describes a joint Denmark-Sweden-Finland evaluation. Germany is not part of it, so NAV’s assumption of common genetic parameters for all countries does not cover German herds. That makes the genotype x country analysis (Chapter 5) more relevant for Germany than for the other three countries.

title: 2  Step 0: genetic parameters and breeding goal
text:
2.3 Genetic correlations

40 of 55 trait pairs have a published source. Index-based values were accepted only from Nordic breeds, genuine estimates from European studies, and recent estimates over old ones. The evidence for every pair is in the evidence workbook.
The other 15 pairs take the values implied by weighted bending (Jorjani et al. 2003). Bending makes the matrix positive definite, which the simulation needs, while moving published values by at most about 0.015. These 15 values are not estimates.
The NUE correlations (milk yield 0.52, protein yield 0.80, milk urea -0.12) all come from one study of grazing Irish cows (Tavernier et al. 2024). This is the weakest input, so Chapter 9 tests how much the conclusions depend on it.







WarningWhy ordinary bending was not used



Ordinary bending shrinks every correlation by the same rule. It would have moved the published milk-protein correlation from 0.86 to 0.74. Weighted bending keeps published values almost fixed and moves the unknown ones instead.
crumbs: 2  Step 0: genetic parameters and breeding goal

title: 2  Step 0: genetic parameters and breeding goal
text:
2.4 The breeding goal
The NTM sub-index weights (May 2026) were used for the sub-indices that have a simulated trait. These carry 64% of the NTM weight for HOL and RDC and 72% for JER; the rest is not simulated. NUE has no published economic value, so two weights were tested on top of NTM: 0.35 (equal to the Saved Feed weight) and 0.75.
Full report: Step 0, genetic parameters. The check of the correlation update is in the update-check report.
crumbs: 2  Step 0: genetic parameters and breeding goal

title: 3  Step 1: founder genomes and burn-in
text:
3.1 Why this step matters
Genomic selection works through linkage disequilibrium between markers and causal loci, and through family structure. If the starting population were a random sample, genomic prediction would look better or worse than it really is. The start population must look like a selected cattle population.
crumbs: 3  Step 1: founder genomes and burn-in

title: 3  Step 1: founder genomes and burn-in
text:
3.2 Key choices

Coalescent founders. Genomes come from MaCS with the cattle demography in AlphaSimR (current effective population size 90; MacLeod et al. 2013), extended to three breeds: the HOL and RDC lineages join 30 generations ago and JER 50 generations ago. These split times are not calibrated to an observed FST.
Genome size. 29 chromosomes (the bovine autosomes), so that genome length is realistic, with 10,005 SNP and 600 founders per breed. The SNP number was chosen to fit a 2-core, 6 GB machine; a 50k version is in the hpc/ folder.
Herds. Single-breed herds, as on CFIT farms.
Burn-in. Selection on milk and protein yield, to reproduce historical yield selection before NUE is considered.
Replicates. Each replicate uses seed 20261031 plus the replicate number and draws its own founders, so the spread between replicates includes founder sampling.







TipPaired comparisons



Within a replicate, every breeding scenario starts from the same founders, burn-in and random seed. A difference between two scenarios is therefore paired, which removes much of the noise when they are compared in Chapter 8.


Full report: Step 1, founders and burn-in.
crumbs: 3  Step 1: founder genomes and burn-in

title: 4  Step 2: genomic prediction
text:
4.1 The models
The five models from BayesR on are fitted to the phenotype corrected for herd x generation means, computed from training cows only. They use only genotyped cows, so they compare with GBLUP and the SNP models, not with single-step. They use their own random-number stream, so adding them leaves the results of the other models unchanged (checked).
MTG2 (Lee and van der Werf 2016) and DMU (Madsen and Jensen 2024) are prepared in the code but not yet run: both are distributed by their authors as executables, and they are added once the programs are available.

title: 4  Step 2: genomic prediction
text:
4.2 How accuracy was measured

Validation. Three-fold cross-validation, plus forward validation in which the youngest cows are predicted from older ones.
Accuracy is the correlation between the estimated and the true breeding value. Only a simulation knows the true value.
Within-breed accuracy is reported, because selection happens within breed. Pooled accuracy is distorted by differences between breed means.







WarningSingle-step in a multi-breed population



The genomic (G) and pedigree (A22) relationship matrices have different bases. Without adjustment, single-step GBLUP gives breed-level offsets in the breeding values. The pipeline tests an adjusted G and breed metafounders (Vitezica et al. 2011; Legarra et al. 2015).

A single-step model was the best or within 0.05 of the best in 10 of 10 trait x validation comparisons (the eight shown here plus NUE in the GxE scenario). In the eight comparisons above, a single-step model had the highest within-breed accuracy every time. It is the only family that also uses the records of cows without genotypes. The five extra models did not improve on GBLUP, the model they compare with:

BayesR, BayesRC and both JWAS models were within 0.05 of GBLUP in all eight comparisons (differences from -0.048 to +0.030).
BayesRC_QTL, with the SNPs next to the largest simulated QTL as the prior set, differed from GBLUP by -0.020 to +0.007. Even a perfect biological prior added nothing here.

title: 5  Step 3: multi-trait models and genotype x country interaction
text:
5.1 Multi-trait models
NUE is expensive to record. If it is genetically correlated with traits that are recorded routinely, those traits can carry information to cows without NUE records. The step fits 11-trait Bayesian models with three structures for the genetic covariances: diagonal (no correlations), unstructured, and factor-analytic.
For cows whose NUE was hidden, NUE accuracy was 0.09 with the unstructured model against 0.01 with the diagonal model. Only the unstructured model gained from the correlations.
crumbs: 5  Step 3: multi-trait models and genotype x country interaction

title: 5  Step 3: multi-trait models and genotype x country interaction
text:
NoteToo few cows for 11 traits



With 1,500 cows, the 11-trait covariance matrix could not be estimated well: heritabilities were pulled towards the prior and genetic correlations shrunk towards zero, although their pattern was recovered. That is one reason why the real CFIT data, with tens of thousands of cows, matter.
crumbs: 5  Step 3: multi-trait models and genotype x country interaction

title: 5  Step 3: multi-trait models and genotype x country interaction
text:
5.2 Genotype x country interaction
One joint evaluation is valid only if the genetic correlation of a trait between countries is high. A correlation below about 0.80 means that bulls re-rank between countries.

Decision rule. GxE is declared only if the likelihood-ratio test has p < 0.05 and the upper 95% limit of the between-country correlation is below 0.80.
Negative control. A dataset simulated without GxE is always analysed as well, to check that the rule does not raise false alarms.
Bayesian check. The same model is fitted with two opposite priors (correlation 0 and 0.95). If the answer follows the prior, the data are uninformative.

title: 6  Step 4: the breeding programme
text:
6.2 Key choices

Evaluation model. SNP-BLUP, solved in its n x n (dual) form to save memory. 04b_model_test.Rmd was designed to compare it with single-step GBLUP inside the programme, but single-step exceeded the memory of the machine used.
Training set. About 6,000 genotyped and phenotyped cows per generation.
Methane weight. -0.5 is the knee of a selection-index sweep in Step 0: the largest methane reduction per unit of NTM given up.
Recorded every generation. Genetic trends, accuracy of the breeding values, the four-path breeder’s equation, and genomic inbreeding.







TipOptimum contribution selection



Optimum contribution selection chooses how many offspring each bull may have, so that genetic gain is as high as possible while the rate of inbreeding stays at a set limit, here 1% per generation (the FAO guideline).


Full reports (replicate 0): NTM, NTM + NUE 0.35, NTM + NUE 0.75, milk urea, methane, optimum contribution, mate allocation, phenotypic selection, model test.

text:
7.2 NUE over time






Figure 7.2: NUE genetic gain from the start of genomic selection under NTM alone and with an NUE weight of 0.35 or 0.75. Lines are means over 10 replicates; ribbons are 95% confidence intervals.

title: 7  Responses and trade-offs
text:
7.3 What the figures show

NTM alone already raises NUE (by 3.3 to 3.4 SD), carried by protein yield, whose genetic correlation with NUE is 0.80.
An NUE weight adds more. At weight 0.35 NUE rises by a further HOL 1.08, JER 0.94 and RDC 0.82 SD.
Methane rises under NTM alone (HOL 1.89, JER 1.60, RDC 2.10 SD), through its positive genetic correlations with yield. NTM has no methane weight. The methane weight reverses most of this rise.
A milk urea weight lowers milk urea but not NUE. This agrees with the weak genetic correlation between the two (-0.12).
Optimum contribution selection halves the rate of inbreeding, from about 1.8 to 2.2% to 0.7 to 1.0% per generation.







Figure 7.3: Genomic inbreeding under NTM + NUE 0.35 with and without optimum contribution selection (mean of 10 replicates).









NoteSimulation and theory agree for NUE



The NUE response relative to NTM alone was compared with selection-index theory. At weight 0.35 they agree closely (HOL 1.32 in the simulation against 1.32 in theory). At 0.75 the simulated gain is smaller than theory, which is consistent with NUE breeding values being less accurate than protein-yield breeding values, whereas theory assumes true breeding values.

title: 8  Statistics and multiple testing
text:
8.1 Paired tests
Within a replicate, all programmes share the same founders, burn-in and random seed. The difference between two programmes is therefore computed within each replicate and tested with a paired t-test over the 10 replicates, once per breed.

title: 8  Statistics and multiple testing
text:
8.4 Which method to read






TipBenjamini-Hochberg is the preferred reading



The study screens many differences rather than confirming one hypothesis, the tests are dependent (the same replicates, correlated traits), and there are only 10 replicates. Bonferroni would hide real differences; uncorrected p-values overstate the evidence. Bonferroni is kept as the conservative bound: a result that passes it is beyond reasonable doubt in this simulation.


Benjamini-Hochberg is proven for independent or positively dependent tests (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995; Benjamini & Yekutieli 2001); it is not guaranteed under every form of dependence.
What changes after correction. The NUE gains, the methane, milk urea and inbreeding effects all hold. The NTM costs of optimum contribution selection and of the milk urea weight, and the apparent NTM gain in Holstein at NUE weight 0.35, do not. They should be read as not established.
All adjusted p-values are in the multiple-testing table and in Tables A to E of the summary report.

title: 9  Sensitivity analyses
text: 9.1 How to read it

title: 9  Sensitivity analyses
text:
Left panel. As the NUE correlations shrink towards zero, the NUE gain under NTM alone falls to about zero. NTM improves NUE only through those correlations.
Right panel. The extra NUE from an explicit weight stays positive in every set, including when NUE is unrelated to every other trait (HOL +1.56 SD).







ImportantThe conclusion



The recommendation to add an NUE weight does not depend on the uncertain NUE correlations. The statement that NTM already improves NUE does.

title: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations
text: 10.1 The plan
crumbs: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations

title: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations
text:
Evaluation. A single-step model for routine evaluation, because it uses cows with CFIT records but no genotypes. In a multi-breed population, the genomic and pedigree relationships must be made compatible first (adjusted G or breed metafounders). Weighted single-step should not be used, because its breeding values were over-dispersed.
Selection index. Add an explicit NUE weight to NTM. NTM alone improves NUE only through its correlations with yield; an explicit weight adds about 0.8 to 1.1 SD more at weight 0.35. Which weight to use is a price decision for the breeding organisation; because the simulated NTM cost is within noise, the cost should be priced from selection-index theory.
No milk urea weight, unless urinary nitrogen or ammonia gets its own value in the breeding goal. A milk urea weight lowered milk urea but did not raise NUE.
Methane. A methane weight of -0.5 reverses most of the rise in methane under NTM, at a cost in NTM value.
One joint evaluation across Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Germany, unless a GxE analysis on real data shows a between-country correlation credibly below 0.80.
Optimum contribution selection at 1% inbreeding per generation. Mate allocation alone lowered final inbreeding but left the rate at 0.8 to 1.2% per generation, above the guideline.
Records. CFIT feed intake for nitrogen intake, plus milk protein and milk urea from routine recording. Predicted NUE is the realistic phenotype; measured urinary nitrogen is not available at scale.
crumbs: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations

title: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations
text:
10.2 Limitations

15 of 55 genetic correlations are implied by bending, not estimated, and many sourced values are proxies or come from other breeds.
All NUE correlations come from one grazing Irish study; confinement-fed Nordic cows may differ.
Only 64 to 72% of the NTM weight is simulated, so absolute EUR values are too large. Comparisons between scenarios are less affected.
10,005 SNP and a 1,500-cow subsample for genomic cross-validation and GxE, because of computing limits.
Methane parameters from Danish Holstein are applied to all breeds.
The NTM costs of the milk urea weight and of optimum contribution selection do not pass correction for multiple testing; more replicates are needed.
crumbs: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations

title: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations
text:
10.3 What real data would add
Genetic correlations of NUE with production, feed efficiency, health, fertility and resilience in Nordic breeds; whether these correlations change across lactation and parity; and GxE estimated on the full population. The pipeline reads all parameters from the params/ folder, so real estimates can replace the literature values directly.
The full list of assumptions and the verification log are in the pipeline notes.
crumbs: 10  Recommended breeding plan and limitations

title: 11  Reproduce the pipeline
text:
11.1 Requirements
R 4.3 or later with AlphaSimR, sommer, BGLR, rrBLUP, nadiv, data.table, ggplot2, knitr and rmarkdown. The script hpc/install_packages.R installs them.
The extra genomic prediction models of Step 2 (extra_models = true) also need:
tools/install_extra_models.sh installs both. MTG2 and DMU are distributed by their authors as executables (MTG2, DMU); DMU is free for research, while commercial use such as routine evaluation needs terms from QGG.

title: 11  Reproduce the pipeline
text:
BayesRCO for BayesR and BayesRC: compiled from source with gfortran.
Julia 1.10 with JWAS 2.4.0. The exact package versions are in tools/julia_env/. Distributions is pinned to 0.25.80, because JWAS 2.4.0 allows StatsBase only up to 0.33 and later Distributions releases do not work with it.

title: 11  Reproduce the pipeline
text:
11.2 Run it
# Quick check of the whole chain at 5% scale
Rscript -e "rmarkdown::render('00_genetic_parameters.Rmd')"
Rscript -e "rmarkdown::render('01_founders_burnin.Rmd', params = list(run_mode = 'TEST'))"

# The full run reported here (144 steps, resumable; each finished step leaves logs/<step>.done)
./queue.sh queue_full_run.txt

# Step 2 again with the extra models (BayesR, BayesRC, JWAS) for the four traits
./queue.sh queue_extra_models.txt

# Rebuild the spreadsheet of replicate results
python3 tools/build_xlsx.py






NoteHow long it takes



On a 2-core, 6 GB machine the full run took about three days: about 80 minutes per founder set, 6 to 9 minutes per burn-in and 24 to 36 minutes per scenario. The 50k-SNP cluster version is in hpc/.

title: 11  Reproduce the pipeline
text:
11.3 Rebuild this website
The figures and tables on this site are drawn from the result files by book/make_figures.Rmd. Then Quarto renders the site into docs/:
cd book && Rscript -e "rmarkdown::render('make_figures.Rmd')" && cd ..
quarto render
